guards.rule: A bath fixture whose height exceeds the sloped-ceiling headroom at its position must not be built as a bathtub; the solver must substitute a shower or a low-profile fixture that fits the available height.
An interior camera of a furnished room must frame the room's main furniture group, not an empty corner; a frame that shows no furniture is a failed view.
An 'empty room' finding on a room whose program lists built furniture is a camera framing error, not a missing-furniture error; fix the camera, do not re-furnish.

A piece whose height exceeds the clear ceiling height at its position (sloped or flat) must not be placed there; the fitter must reject or relocate any piece that pokes through the roof or ceiling, and a bathroom under a low mansard slope must be given a shower, not a bathtub.
An interior camera must not frame a black or empty volume; if the room's ceiling is too low for the camera to stand, the camera must be moved to a free point with headroom or the view removed.
A soft-seat model whose parts stand more than 1 cm apart is a build defect; the build stage must join the facing bodies of the model before the piece is placed.
A soft-seat model whose back or arm stands more than 5 mm from its seat is a build defect; the build stage must slide every back, back cushion and arm against its seat before the piece is placed.

Scene check S1 failures on a level indicate build-stage geometry defects (pieces not resting on the floor, parts detached, or pieces poking through walls); the build stage must be rerun to resolve them.

Scene check S2 failures on a level indicate build-stage geometry defects (pieces not resting on the floor, parts detached, or pieces poking through walls); the build stage must be rerun to resolve them.
A scene check that fails on a level is a build-stage defect: re-run the build stage for that level so the geometry is regenerated and re-checked.

When a seating piece is wedged behind the back of its group and every single rotation is refused (it would face a wall or lose its group), the cause is the room's overall seating layout, not one piece: re-solve the room's AI pieces as a group so the seating cluster is re-placed coherently.

When a TV unit is placed behind the back of a seating piece and rotating it would pull it off its wall (F3) while swapping its model is refused, the cause is the room's seating/TV layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the TV unit lands on a wall facing the sofa.
A piece that crosses a room outline by 0.02 m or less (a few centimetres of its depth) is within tolerance and is not a real finding.

When a coffee table overlaps an armchair and every move of the table is refused (it re-overlaps or hits the max-tries limit), the cause is the seating cluster's spacing: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the table and chairs are placed with clearance.

When a piece's front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door and no single edit can open the path, the cause is the room's circulation layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the walkway is clear.
When a large sofa's front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door, the cause is the room's circulation layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the walkway is clear.

When a seating piece is wedged behind the back of its group and rotating it would face a wall, the cause is the room's overall seating layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the seating cluster is re-placed coherently.

When a TV unit is placed behind the back of a seating piece and rotating it would pull it off its wall while moving it breaks the sofa axis, the cause is the room's seating/TV layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the TV unit lands on a wall facing the sofa.
A stove or hob that is part of a kitchen counter run (built into the worktop) is not checked for back-on-wall clearance; the run's own depth against the wall is its position.
A kitchen counter run must leave at least 0.90 m of clear aisle in front of it; if the drawn counter position leaves less, the AI pieces (island, fridge, stools) are re-solved to open the aisle.
A kitchen counter run must leave at least 0.90 m of clear aisle in front of it; if the drawn counter position leaves less, the AI pieces are re-solved to open the aisle.
An armchair in a seating group must face the group's centre (coffee table or sofa); if the drawn position locks it facing away, the AI pieces are re-solved to orient it.
An armchair's front free zone must be clear of other pieces; if the drawn position locks it against a neighbour, the AI pieces are re-solved.
A dining chair needs at least 0.81 m from the table edge to the wall or piece behind it; if the drawn table position leaves less, the AI dining pieces are re-solved.
An armchair in a seating group must face the group's centre; if the drawn position locks it facing away, the AI pieces are re-solved.
An armchair must not stand behind the back of a sofa facing it; it should be on the opposite side of the coffee table or at an angle to the group.
An armchair's front free zone must be clear; if the drawn position locks it against a neighbour, the AI pieces are re-solved.
A double bed needs at least 0.60 m of free aisle on at least one side; if the drawn bed position leaves less, the AI pieces are re-solved to open the aisle.
A wardrobe needs at least 0.80 m of free space in front for the doors to open; if the drawn position leaves less, the AI pieces are re-solved.
A drawn shower with a depth below 0.70 m is a misread; the depth is corrected to the minimum product size (0.70 m) if the room allows.

A bed placed against a wall with a side gap under 0.60 m must be swapped to a narrower model (or the nightstand removed) so the side clearance meets the 0.60 m minimum; a swap to a lower-rated model is refused, so pick the narrowest model in the project's style chain.

A wardrobe whose front clearance is under 0.80 m and whose drawn wall span is blocked by doors/windows must be slid along its wall (or to the nearest free span) so the door opens; if no span within 1.2 m of the drawn place is free, the room layout must be re-solved rather than forcing the piece off its wall.
A bed with a side gap under 0.60 m that cannot be fixed by moving (headboard must stay on the wall) must be swapped to a narrower model in the project's style chain.
A wardrobe with under 0.80 m front clearance that cannot be slid along its wall (no free span) must be moved to the nearest free place in the room so the door opens.
A piece blocking the free zone in front of a sofa must be moved (or removed) so the sofa's front use zone is clear; the blocking piece, not the sofa, is the cause.
A coffee table not in front of the sofa must be moved to the sofa's front use zone (0.40-0.60 m from the seat front), aligned with the sofa's long side.
An armchair more than 2.50 m from the coffee table or more than 30° off its axis must be moved into the seating group (within 2.50 m, within 30° of the table axis).
An armchair standing behind the back of its group's anchor must be rotated to face the group (the anchor's front), not the anchor's back.

A drawn coffee table that is not in front of the sofa and cannot be moved more than 0.3 m (drawn lock) must have the sofa moved to the table, or the table re-anchored, so the table sits in the sofa's front zone.
A flat 2D image of furniture standing on the floor is a rendering error, not a real piece; it must be removed (or replaced by a real 3D model of the same type).
An armchair standing behind the back of its group's anchor must be rotated to face the group.
A dining chair with under 0.81 m behind it (to the wall or a piece) must be moved so the pull-out clearance meets 0.81 m.
A tv_unit whose back is not on a wall (more than 0.05 m off) must be moved to a wall so its back rests on it.
Armchairs facing the back of a tv_unit that is off the wall are a symptom of the tv_unit's position; move the tv_unit to the wall so the armchairs face its front.

When multiple pieces in a room face each other's backs (a seating group with reversed orientations), the room's AI pieces must be re-laid out as a group so the seating faces the tv_unit/anchor, not each other's backs.
A built piece must not cross its room outline; when the assigned model is too deep for the wall bay, swap to a model whose depth fits the bay.
A drawn sofa footprint whose width exceeds its depth (an L or corner shape) must be typed as sofa_corner, not sofa, so the built model matches the drawn shape.
A seating group's front use zone must be kept clear; when a piece blocks the sofa's front, the room is re-laid out so the group faces open floor.
A seating group's front use zone must be kept clear; when a piece blocks an armchair's front, the room is re-laid out so the group faces open floor.
A kitchen run must leave at least 0.90 m of aisle in front of the counter; when the room is too narrow for the drawn run plus aisle, the run is re-solved on the longest free wall span.
A seating group's members must face the group; when an armchair does not face its group, the room is re-laid out so the group is coherent.
A double bed must have at least 0.60 m of free walkway on each side; when the room is too narrow for the bed plus two 0.60 m aisles, the bed is placed against a wall with one side open.
The agent stage must not drop decor pieces (potted plants, side tables, armchairs) that the decor stage placed; every decor piece is either built or explicitly removed with a reason.
The agent stage must not drop a placed decor piece without recording it; a piece present after the decor stage and absent after the agent stage is a loss to be restored, not silently removed.

A stove (hob) that is built into a kitchen counter run is part of that run's model and must not be emitted as a separate scene object; the build stage must suppress a standalone stove object when the stove is a member of a built-in kitchen run, and the conservation check must not flag the run's integrated hob as a missing object.

A kitchen sink that is built into a counter run is part of that run's model and must not be emitted as a separate scene object; the build stage must suppress a standalone sink object when the sink is a member of a built-in kitchen run, and the conservation check must not flag the run's integrated sink as a missing object.

When a drawn piece is a duplicate of a larger drawn piece of the same type (one floor lamp drawn twice, not two), the smaller duplicate is a detail of the larger one and is correctly left out; the reading stage must not flag a same-type duplicate drawn inside its partner as a lost piece.
none

A stair drawn on a dedicated stair layer (e.g. A-MERDIVEN) is a drawing of the stair the model already builds from its own stair reading; it is not a lost element and must not be reported as unused geometry.
A stair elevation/section layer (e.g. A-merdiven görünüş) is a drawing of the stair the model already builds; it is not a lost element and must not be reported as unused geometry.
A decorative sanitary-ware layer (e.g. Deko_Vitrifiye) is a drawing of the bathroom fixtures the model already builds; it is not a lost element and must not be reported as unused geometry.
A sanitary-ware layer (e.g. Piu_Vitrifiye) is a drawing of the bathroom fixtures the model already builds; it is not a lost element and must not be reported as unused geometry.

A toilet's centre must be at least 0.38 m from any side wall or fixture; when the drawn position violates this in a room too small to re-place it, the finding is a genuine clearance conflict to flag, not a model error.
A shower needs at least 0.53 m clear in front; when the room geometry leaves only 0.28 m, the finding is a genuine clearance conflict to flag, not a model error.
A shower needs at least 0.53 m clear in front; when the room geometry leaves only 0.05 m, the finding is a genuine clearance conflict to flag, not a model error.
A bathtub needs at least 0.53 m clear in front; when the room geometry leaves only 0.28 m, the finding is a genuine clearance conflict to flag, not a model error.
An interior camera must show the room's primary fixtures; if a fixture is not visible, the camera pose is wrong, not the fixture.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame its main fixtures (basin, toilet, shower/bath) so the room reads as functional, not a bare corner.
A bedroom's layout must keep the bed as the anchor with the wardrobe's front clearance (>=0.80 m) satisfied; a layout that drops the bed for a desk is not a bedroom.
A bedroom render must show the bed as the anchor; a camera that crops the bed out is not a valid view of the room.
The exterior/site environment must carry real ground cover and planting so the scene reads as a finished home, not a flat grey placeholder.
An opening must be cut through its wall; a door ray that still hits the wall means the cut was not applied.
The wall-item/decor pass must not place a hung decor piece over an existing wall item (basin, mirror, cabinet); it must raise it, move it along the wall, or drop it.
The wall-item/decor pass must not hang a piece over a window opening; it must move it to a free wall span or drop it.

A hung wall decor item must never occupy the same wall span and height band as a built wall fixture (basin, mirror, cabinet); the decor pass must test each decor item against every wall item on the same wall and re-place or drop it on collision.

A hung wall decor item must never occupy the same wall span and height band as a built wall fixture; the decor pass must test each decor item against every wall item on the same wall and re-place or drop it on collision.
A tall cabinet placed under a sloped ceiling must be a model whose height fits the local ceiling clearance; the fit pass must reject any model taller than the headroom at the piece's position.

A living room with a long blank outer wall (no window or door) must have a window added on that wall at the reading stage; the facade pass must not leave a habitable room's outer wall without daylight or access.
Every project must include a frontal exterior camera square to the entrance (+y) facade at eye height (1.5-1.7 m), outside the building envelope, showing the entrance door.
When the terrain slope exceeds 1:3, the site pass must build a retaining edge (retaining wall or stepped plinth) along the steep side; a steep slope without a retaining edge is a site defect.

A bathroom washbasin must be built as part of a complete bathroom set (basin + mirror + cabinet); a bare bowl on a counter with no mirror is an unfinished bathroom and the fit pass must add the missing mirror.
An outdoor terrace must be furnished with a terrace lounge group (seating + table + decor) so it reads as a finished outdoor space, not a bare slab with plants.

The entrance door must be clearly defined and accessible: the reading stage must verify that the entrance door leads to a defined interior space (not a dead-end wall) and that the approach (ramp/steps) terminates at the door leaf.
A sofa placed on an outdoor terrace must use an outdoor-rated model (weather-resistant), not an upholstered indoor model; the fit pass must reject indoor upholstery models for outdoor rooms.
A coffee table placed on an outdoor terrace must use an outdoor-rated model (weather-resistant), not an indoor model; the fit pass must reject indoor models for outdoor rooms.

An exterior site/aerial view is not required to show every facade window; the K1 'must show' obligation applies only to interior views and to the dedicated frontal/entrance exterior views, not to the aerial site view.

An exterior camera that must show a facade frontally is placed outside the building envelope, at eye height, on the open side of that facade; a pose that lands inside the building or under the roof is refused and the camera is re-solved from the free stretch of the view line.

A drawn bed footprint wider than about 2.0 m is a misread (it includes the headboard, a nightstand or a wall line); the reading caps the bed at a real product width and flags the excess, and the fit stage never resizes a bed beyond a real product size.
Furniture placed on a balcony or terrace is drawn only from outdoor-rated library models (weather-resistant, matching the terrace's style family); an indoor model is refused for an outdoor room.

A bathroom render must show a mirror over the washbasin and a styled (accent or layered) wall finish behind it; a bare flat-tile wall with no mirror is a failed bathroom view and the camera must be re-posed to frame the basin and mirror.
A balcony/terrace render must read as a designed outdoor living space (rug, lighting, styled view), not a bare grey-box terrace with only a chair and a plant.

A drawn piece whose cluster exceeds 4.5 m on a side is a group of pieces, not a single furniture item; the reading must split it into its member pieces and type each, rather than leaving one oversized untyped cluster that nothing builds.
A hall/corridor camera must be posed to show an open, lit, furnished room beyond a door, not a closed door leaf and a bare wall.
The facade must follow the family's facade scheme (e.g. white render over a stone base), not be clad in stone from base to eaves.
A bathroom's set must include a tall_cabinet (storage) on every level; a bathroom missing it is incomplete.
A sofa with no front set must be given the front the code suggests (towards its partner across the open floor) so it is oriented correctly.
A bathroom camera must be posed to show the open, lit, furnished room, not a closed door leaf filling the frame.
A bathroom camera must render the furnished room, not a black/empty frame; if the only view is empty, re-pose it to show the room's pieces.
An interior camera must frame the room's anchor piece (the bed in a bedroom); a pose that crops it out is refused.
A camera must not crop a foreground piece off the frame; the pose is chosen to show the named pieces whole.
A bedroom render should show its exit door so the room reads as connected to the plan.
A bathroom camera must frame the room as a whole (vanity, toilet, cabinet), not a single fixture in isolation.

When the documents draw a bathtub block for a bathroom, the built fixture must be a bathtub; a shower is only built when the drawing shows a shower tray. The retype size table must not override a drawn fixture type.
A shoe_cabinet is only placed at an entrance (a hall that has an outside door); on an interior landing or top-floor hall the storage piece is a console_table or sideboard, not a shoe cabinet.
A terrace larger than about 10 m2 must be furnished with a seating set (terrace_lounge), not a single chair.
A camera must not frame only a bare wall or corner; it must show the room's fixtures or furniture.
The facade slot is the main outer wall above the stone base; it takes the family's render (white plaster) unless the brief names another facade material.
A bathroom of this size must include a tall_cabinet; the bathroom_set group is completed with what it misses.

When an opening's door ray hits a wall but the opening already lies on the wall (offset 0.000 m), the wall must be cut through at the opening's location; the geometry stage must cut the wall for every opening that lies on it, not only for openings offset from it.

A wall-hung washbasin is mounted at its working height (rim ~0.85 m); the S1 lowest-point check must accept the mounted height rather than flag the gap to the floor, and swap_model fit rules must not reject a correctly-mounted basin on caps/height.
A small table_coffee/armchair overlap (<=0.15 m2) that no free placement clears must be resolved by shrinking the table to a smaller model or nudging the armchair, not left as an overlap.
An armchair that clashes in style with the sofa and sits >2.5 m from the coffee table must be re-placed into the seating group or removed, not left as a mismatched, mis-oriented piece.

A nightstand built below the library level (parametric mesh) must be swapped to a real library model that passes the fit rules (caps, height) and the project's style chain; the fit rules must accept a correctly-sized nightstand.
A toilet built below the library level (parametric mesh) must be swapped to a real library model that passes the fit rules (caps, height); the fit rules must accept a correctly-sized toilet.
A sofa whose back is >0.10 m off a wall and has no free wall span within 1.2 m must be re-placed to a free wall span or the room re-laid out, not left floating.
A wardrobe with <0.80 m free in front that cannot be moved without breaking the room outline must be swapped to a shallower model or the room re-laid out.
A bed_double with <0.60 m free along a side that cannot be moved without breaking the room must be swapped to a narrower model or the room re-laid out.
A kitchen_run that is planned but has no object in the scene must be built; the place_group solver must not refuse to build a kitchen_run that the room already has as a drawn group.
A wardrobe with <0.80 m free in front that cannot be moved to a free wall span must be swapped to a shallower model or the room re-laid out.
A living room with >3 m of outer wall and no window or door (a blank facade) must have a window or door added, or the room re-typed, to break the blank facade.
A shoe_cabinet on a top-floor landing (a twin of a misread piece) must be re-typed to a piece that fits its size and room, or removed if it does not belong.
A tv_unit that stands behind the back of an armchair and is >0.10 m off a wall must be re-placed to face the sofa and sit on a wall, or the room re-laid out.
A wardrobe that reaches <=0.05 m2 through the room outline (up to <=0.020 m deep) is within tolerance and must not be flagged by F9; the F5 rule must accept this case.

Rule C1 (furniture placement) must require that every seating piece's front use zone be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door or opening; a piece whose front zone is cut off by another piece or a wall is a placement error, not a detail.
Rule S4 (bathroom fixture spacing) must require a minimum of 0.38 m clearance from the side wall or adjacent fixture for every toilet; a toilet closer than this is a spacing error.

Rule F4 (furniture orientation) must require that the free zone in front of every seating piece be unobstructed; a piece whose front zone is blocked by another piece is an orientation/placement error.
Rule F4 must require that the free zone in front of a sofa be unobstructed; a sofa whose front zone is blocked by another piece is a placement error.
Rule E1 (envelope) must flag any outer wall span longer than 3 m with no window or door as a blank facade requiring an opening.
Full-height windows in living rooms must be dressed with layered curtains (a sheer behind a heavier drape) so the glass is never left bare in a render.
Coffee tables must be styled with a small set of props (books, a vase, a bowl) so the surface is never rendered bare.
Living rooms must use layered lighting: a warm floor or table lamp in addition to the main pendant, so the room is not lit by a single cold source.
Interior bathroom cameras must be placed at the room's far corner looking across the room, showing the tub, basin and toilet together; a pose pressed against a wall corner is invalid.
Interior cameras must never be placed inside a door swing or pressed against a door leaf; the door must not fill the frame.
Bathroom renders must include styled surfaces: accessories on the basin, a towel, and an accent wall or warm light, so the room is not bare and flat.
Bathroom windows must be dressed with a sheer or a short drape so the glass is not left bare.
Interior hall cameras must be placed at one end of the hall looking down its length, showing the floor and the main group; a pose pressed against a wall showing only a picture frame is invalid.
Bedrooms must have a textured feature wall (fluted or slatted panelling) behind the bed; a plain flat headboard panel is not acceptable in a styled render.
Desks in bedrooms must be styled as a console (art, vases, books) rather than dominated by a laptop, so the room reads as a bedroom, not a generic office.
Beds must be rendered with layered bedding: a duvet, euro shams, and decorative cushions, not just a flat sheet and a single runner.
Bathroom doors must match the room's neutral, modern palette; a warm, prominent wood door with a large handle is out of place.
Interior hall cameras must show the room as a whole from a corner, not focus on the side of a single piece of furniture.
Armchairs in a living room must share the same style family and a compatible colour palette with the sofas; clashing eras or colours are not acceptable.
Every piece must be a 3D model; a flat 2D image standing on the floor is a critical rendering error and must be replaced.
Dining chairs and tables must be from the same style family; a white spindle chair with a round pedestal table does not match a modern living room.
A balcony or terrace with seating must be styled with at least a rug or planter and a light source so it reads as a finished outdoor room, not a bare slab.
An interior or balcony camera must frame the room's main furniture and its boundary (railing, windows), not a bare corner or the floor.
When the reference style mixes white and wood, at least one interior wall slot must carry a warm wood look so the palette is not all grey.
Upper-floor living and bedroom windows should carry soft furnishings (curtains or blinds) so they read as lived-in, not bare openings.
An exterior camera must be a clear eye-level (1.5-1.7 m) or drone shot of the facade; it must not be obstructed by a car, roof, or interior.
A finding that names a piece id not present in the built model is a false alarm; the inspector should only flag pieces that exist.
A flush ceiling light must be at least 2.5 m from a pendant light; if they are closer, one must be removed or moved.
A dining set should mix a bench with upholstered or wood chairs, not repeat a single molded plastic chair.
A shoe cabinet must be a believable, styled piece of furniture, not a crude low-poly metal frame.
An accent armchair should match the room's neutral palette; a second loud accent (orange) that clashes with the teal chair is not allowed.
A side table must be a believable piece of furniture, not a toy-like disc with random pegs.
A terrace with seating must include a table and cushions so it reads as a usable, styled outdoor space.
An armchair's back and arms must be within 5 mm of its seat; a model with a 2.4 cm gap is not acceptable.
A finding that applies an armchair geometry check to a potted_plant is a false alarm; the check should only apply to the correct piece type.
A feature wall (slatted wood or paneling) is required behind the dining area and main living wall to add depth and sophistication.
A bedroom's desk chair must be a residential, upholstered or wood model in the project's style chain, never a black leather or mesh corporate office chair.
A bedroom's desk chair must be a residential, upholstered or wood model in the project's style chain, never a black mesh corporate office chair.
An interior hall camera must frame the hall's circulation (stair, doors) with the storage as context, never let a single wardrobe fill half the frame and hide the room.
A living room's seating group (sofa, armchairs, lounge chair) must share one style and a coherent colour family; a brown leather armchair is not mixed with a white boxy sofa and a black lounge chair.
Every exterior and terrace render must sit in a finished, landscaped site (grass, a path, a hedge or fence, trees, a front court), never a flat textureless void or grey-box ground.
An outdoor terrace/balcony floor must carry a designed outdoor finish (decking, stone or tile), never a bare untextured grey slab.
Every exterior render must sit in a finished, landscaped site under a warm, directional sun (not flat grey light), so materials read with depth.
The house facade must carry a designed cladding (wood, stone or render) with landscape integration, never a sterile grey-box massing study.
A stone-clad wall must use a stone look with depth and variation (ashlar, ledgestone, rubble), never a flat repetitive placeholder texture.
A hall shoe cabinet must be a closed, finished piece (doors, styling) in the project's style, never a bare open-cubby parametric grid.
An interior camera must frame the room's anchor furniture (the bed in a bedroom, the counter in a kitchen), not a bare corner; if the anchor is out of frame the view is not of that room.
The view outside a window must show the designed site (planting, hedges, paving), not a flat untextured field; the site model must carry the landscaping the plan draws.
A kitchen counter's worktop must carry its small appliances and styling (kettle, plant, bowl) as part of the kitchen run; a bare worktop is an incomplete kitchen set.
Door and frame finishes must sit in the same material family as the surrounding joinery; a dark heavy door against light wood slats reads as a mismatch.

Every living room must carry at least one statement light (pendant, floor lamp or recessed downlight) so the render shows layered warm light; a flat evenly lit room is a missing light layer, not a wrong model.
An outdoor terrace floor must be a finished surface (decking, pavers, outdoor rug), not a bare concrete slab with a drain; the ground material slot must carry the terrace finish.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's main fixtures (shower, toilet, basin) from a position with headroom, not a close-up of one corner.
A bathroom camera must not be pressed against a door leaf; it must frame the room's main fixtures from a free point with headroom.
A bedroom camera must frame the bed and its nightstand, the room's anchor; a view that shows only the desk reads as an office, not a bedroom.
A bedroom camera must not be positioned at the door frame cutting off the room; it must frame the bed and nightstands from a free point with headroom.
A bathroom camera must frame the room as a whole from a free point with headroom, not a tight close-up of one corner.
A hall camera must frame the hall's volume and its features (shoe cabinet, stair, accent wall), not a blank corner and wall.
A kitchen camera must frame the counter and its main appliances, not a bare shell with the appliances cut off.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, basin) from a free point with headroom, not a close-up of a corner and a switch plate.
A bedroom camera must not be buried at the foot of the bed; it must frame the bed and its nightstand from a free point with headroom.
A hall camera must frame the hall's volume and its features (shoe cabinet, doors), not a close-up of a wall and a picture frame.
An interior camera must frame the room's main pieces level and in full; a tilted, cropped grey-box view is a camera failure, not a furniture one.
A room's furniture must read as one coherent style; a chaotic mix of mid-century, modern and generic models is a fit failure the furniture agent must resolve.
A render must never contain a flat 2D image standing in for a 3D object; a literal picture of a table on the floor is a build failure.
A room's furniture must read as one coherent style; a catalogue of mismatched pieces is a fit failure the furniture agent must resolve.
Every drawn furniture piece must be typed by a rule or model; a piece left 'unknown' with no explanation is a reading failure that must be resolved before the run ends.
A decor item that cannot rest on its host within tolerance is correctly dropped; the host's top surface must be flat and clear.
A fixture under a sloped ceiling is capped at the slope height at its footprint; the cap is independent of the drawn size check, so a size refusal must not block the height fix.

When one room outline carries the labels of two or more rooms, the reading must split it at the missing wall before room assignment; a label with no matching room outline is a lost-room signal, not a duplicate.
A balcony or terrace with drawn furniture must have that furniture built and visible; an empty outdoor room is a fit failure, not a camera failure.
A stair opening in a hall or landing that drops to a lower level must be built with a guardrail or barrier along its open edge; the guard is part of the stair's set, not an optional detail.
A fixture under a sloped ceiling must be a model whose height fits the headroom at its position; the shower's height is checked against the roof, not just its drawn footprint.
An interior camera must be posed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main group; a black frame means the pose is inside geometry and must be re-picked.
A soft seat's facing bodies must be joined so no part stands more than 1 cm apart; the build stage's join step is responsible for this.
A soft seat's back, back cushion and arms must rest against its seat with no gap over 5 mm; the build stage's rest plan is responsible for this.
Scene geometry checks (S1) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S2) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S4) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S6) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
A scene check that fails on a level must be re-run after the level's pieces are corrected; the build stage owns the scene assembly.
When an armchair's orientation is refused because rotating it breaks its group facing, the whole seating group must be re-solved so the armchair faces the group and the coffee table.
A tv_unit that stands behind the back of a seat and cannot be rotated without leaving the room outline must be re-placed by the room solver so its back is on a wall and it faces the seating.
A wardrobe that pokes through the room outline by a few centimetres should be swapped for a model whose depth fits the wall bay.
When a coffee table overlaps an armchair and every single move is refused, the seating group must be re-solved as a unit so the table clears the chairs.
An armchair whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door must be re-placed by the room solver so the walkway is clear.
A sofa_corner whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door must be re-placed by the room solver so the walkway is clear.
When an armchair's orientation is refused because rotating it breaks its group facing or faces a wall, the whole seating group must be re-solved.
A tv_unit that stands behind the back of a seat and cannot be rotated (back off wall) or swapped (fit rules) must be re-placed by the room solver against a wall facing the seating.
When a coffee table overlaps an armchair and every single move is refused, the seating group must be re-solved as a unit.
A stove whose back is a few centimetres off the wall is a misread centre; the code should snap it to the nearest valid wall spot.
A kitchen aisle narrower than 0.90 m in front of the counter must be re-solved by the room solver so the run is placed to give the required aisle.

A wardrobe (or any storage with a door or drawer front) placed against a wall must keep at least 0.80 m of clear floor in front of its opening face; the solver must reject any wall span shorter than the piece plus that clearance and, when no span fits, flag the room for a smaller or different storage piece rather than placing it with a blocked front.
A seating group's front clearance must be kept free of other pieces; the solver must not place a piece inside the front use zone of a sofa or armchair.
A nightstand must not stand in front of a window sill; it belongs at the head of the bed on the free side.
A dining table must not stand in front of a window sill; it belongs away from the glazing.
A chair must not stand in front of a window sill; it belongs at the table, away from the glazing.
An armchair must face the seating group, not stand behind the back of another piece.
A tv_unit must have its back on a wall; it must not float in the middle of the room.
A sofa's long side is its front; it must not be turned 90° against its product size.
An armchair's front clearance must be kept free of other pieces.
A piece placed by the decor stage must survive the agent stage; if the agent drops it, it must be re-added.

A stove that is a member of a kitchen run (module:kitchen_counter:kitchen_run) must be built as part of that run's model, not as a standalone object; the build stage must emit the run's full model (counter, sink, stove) so every planned member has a scene object.

A sink_kitchen that is a member of a kitchen run (module:kitchen_counter:kitchen_run) must be built as part of that run's model, not as a standalone object; the build stage must emit the run's full model (counter, sink, stove) so every planned member has a scene object.

When two drawn pieces of the same type overlap by more than 30% and one is clearly inside the other, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the same object, not a second piece; the larger is kept and the smaller is dropped as a detail.

When two drawn pieces of the same type overlap by more than 15% and one is clearly inside the other, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the same object, not a second piece; the larger is kept and the smaller is dropped as a detail.
A small piece drawn 80% or more inside a larger seating piece (armchair, sofa) is its seat cushion or built-in element, not a separate piece; it is dropped as a detail of the larger piece.

A room whose program is a stair core (stair fills the room, no free floor point) is not given an interior camera; it is shown by the adjacent hall's view instead, and the camera stage must skip it rather than report it as a lost view.

A drawn block in a kitchen whose size matches a small appliance (roughly 0.2-0.6 m) that the furniture vocabulary does not type must be recorded with an explicit 'appliance, not modelled' note (or a dedicated appliance type) so it is neither silently dropped nor left unexplained.

A layer whose name is a stair section or elevation view (A-MERDIVEN, A-merdiven görünüş) is a detail view, not plan furniture: the reading classifies it as a detail view and feeds it to the stair reader, and the ledger does not flag it as lost when the stair it documents is built.

A layer whose name is a decorative or sanitary fixture detail view (Deko_Vitrifiye, Piu_Vitrifiye) is a detail view, not plan furniture: the reading classifies it as a detail view and the ledger does not flag it as lost.
A stove drawn with a small gap behind it (its back parallel to the wall) belongs on the wall: the reading snaps its back onto the wall instead of leaving a visible gap.
A shower drawn with a small gap behind it (its back parallel to the wall) belongs on the wall: the reading snaps its back onto the wall instead of leaving a visible gap.
A toilet whose centre is closer than 0.38 m to a side wall or fixture is misread: the reading moves it to the nearest valid spot that gives the required side clearance.
A shower with less than 0.53 m clear in front is misread: the reading moves it to the nearest valid spot that gives the required front clearance.

A toilet is placed so its centre is at least 0.38 m from any side wall or fixture; if the drawn position cannot meet this, the fixture is moved to the nearest valid spot rather than swapped for a model that still fails the clearance.
A bathtub must have at least 0.53 m clear in front; if the drawn position cannot meet this, the fixture is moved to the nearest valid spot.
A shower must have at least 0.53 m clear in front; if the drawn position cannot meet this, the fixture is moved to the nearest valid spot.
An interior camera of a bathroom must show the room's main fixtures (washbasin, toilet, shower/bathtub) so the render reads as a functional bathroom.
A bedroom must show its bed as the anchor; if the bed cannot be placed with the required clearances (0.60 m along the sides, headboard on a wall), the room is re-laid out so the bed fits.
An interior camera of a bathroom must show the room's main fixtures (toilet, shower) so the render reads as a functional bathroom.
An interior camera of a balcony/terrace must show the room's main furniture (seating, side table) so the render reads as a designed outdoor living space.
An interior camera of a bathroom must show the room's main fixtures (toilet, washbasin, shower) so the render reads as a functional bathroom.
An interior camera of a bedroom must show the bed as the anchor so the render reads as a bedroom.
An interior camera of a bathroom must show the room's main fixtures (toilet, bathtub, washbasin) so the render reads as a functional bathroom.
An interior camera of a wet room must frame its fixtures (basin, toilet, shower/bath); a view that omits the basin makes the room read as unfinished.
A kitchen's run must be completed with its missing members (fridge, sink, stove, counter); a run without a fridge is not a kitchen.
A bedroom must be furnished as a bedroom (bed, nightstands, wardrobe); a desk-and-chair layout without a visible bed is a misread of the room's program.
An exterior render must show a real ground plane and site context (trees, hedge, court); a flat grey gradient reads as a placeholder.
Every opening must be cut through its wall; an opening whose ray hits the wall is not built.
A wall-mounted decor item must not overlap a wall fixture (basin, mirror, cabinet) on the same wall; the wall-item pass must raise it, move it along the wall, or drop it.
A wall-mounted decor item must not hang over a window opening; the wall-item pass must move it to a free wall span or drop it.

A hung decor item must never be placed on the wall span occupied by a washbasin or its mirror; the resolve pass must skip that span and use the next free wall, or omit the item if no free span exists.
Any outer wall span of a habitable room longer than 3 m must contain at least one window or door; the layout stage must add an opening if the drawing does not provide one.
Every project must include at least one frontal exterior camera view of the main entrance facade.
If the terrain slope is steeper than 1:3, the build stage must include a retaining edge or stepped foundation to support the structure.
Outdoor terrace furniture must use models rated for outdoor use (weather-resistant materials).
Indoor lighting fixtures (floor lamps) must not be placed on outdoor terraces; use outdoor-rated lighting instead.
Indoor storage furniture (bookshelves) must not be placed on outdoor terraces.
The inspector must read the room id of the target piece from the facts before judging its placement; a piece in an indoor living room is not on the terrace.

Every exterior door must be rendered with a modelled leaf and frame that match the window frames' material, and the space beyond an exterior door must be lit and textured (not a dark void) in the render.
Every door leaf and frame must be assigned a material that matches the project's window frame material (e.g. light wood) so that doors do not read as placeholder slabs.

A bathroom shower or bathtub model must include visible taps, a drain, and at least one accessory (towel rail or shelf) in its render; if the library model lacks these, the building stage must add them as separate fixtures or choose a model that includes them.
Every washbasin in a bathroom must be rendered with a mirror above it; if the library model does not include a mirror, the building stage must place a mirror as a separate fixture above the basin.
Every interior camera view of a room must show at least one door or window of that room, so the viewer can orient themselves.

Every exterior camera view must be positioned outside the building envelope, at a distance of at least 1.5 m from the nearest facade, at eye height (1.6 m) or an aerial height, and must not be under the roof overhang.
Every exterior wall, including retaining walls, must be assigned a material that matches the building's facade material so that no bare concrete slabs are visible.
Every bathroom must have a complete bathroom_set including a mirror above the washbasin and a towel rail; if the set is incomplete, the building stage must add the missing members.
The inspector must verify that the bathroom_set members are actually missing before flagging a missing_member finding; if the set is complete, the finding is a false alarm.
Every interior camera view of a bathroom must show the main fixtures (washbasin, toilet, shower/bathtub) so the room reads as designed.

Every bathroom must have a mirror above the washbasin and at least one styled surface (accent wall, shelf, or accessory); if the library models do not include these, the building stage must add them as separate fixtures.

Every outdoor scene must include textured ground (grass, paving, or gravel), at least 3 trees or shrubs with visible foliage, and a horizon that is not a hard line; the render stage must use high-quality ground and vegetation assets.

Every outdoor furniture piece must use a model that matches the project's style (e.g. scandinavian, modern) and has visible texture or design detail; plain generic models are not acceptable for outdoor scenes.
Every terrace or balcony must have a complete terrace_lounge group (at least 2 seating pieces, 1 table, and 2 plants) so it reads as a designed outdoor space.

A kitchen counter (kitchen_counter) is built at its standard working height (top at 0.90-0.95 m) regardless of the drawn footprint's height; a drawn counter taller than its working height is a misread of a tall unit or a wall cabinet, not a counter, and must be retyped or resized, never built as a counter at the drawn height.

A site area labelled as a pool (havuz) in the documents must be built as a pool outline in the model; if the site holds multiple pools, each documented pool area is built with its own outline and water surface, not left as an unbuilt label.
A site area labelled as a sunning terrace (guneslenme alani) in the documents must be built as a paved terrace outline in the model, not left as an unbuilt label.

A site area labelled as a parking area (otopark) in the documents must be built as a paved parking outline in the model, and at least one car model must be placed on it to show it is a parking area, not left as an unbuilt label with no cars.
Every interior door leaf is rendered open against its swing side by default; only entrance and terrace doors are closed.
A bathroom render must frame the vanity, mirror, shower and towel storage, not a bare wall above the tub.
A hall render must show the furnished room beyond, not be dominated by closed door slabs.
A living room must carry its full seating group (sculptural armchairs, round coffee table, lit TV console), not a plain sofa set.
A paved strip at the foot of a long glazed facade must run the full length of the facade, not stop short at one end.
The facade scheme is white render over a stone base, not stone from base to eaves.
In front of a glazed ground-floor facade the site must be a flat pale paved strip, not a raised walled terrace box.
A paved drive or stair path must lead on to the plot edge or a street, not end at the lawn.
An entrance canopy must carry a fascia, soffit and tie rods or brackets, not be a bare slab stuck out of the wall.
A house on a plot must show fenced neighbouring plots and a road coming to it; the drive must lead somewhere.
A drawn piece over 4.5 m on a side is a group of pieces, not a single furniture item; it must be split into its members and typed individually, not left untyped.
A door under a sloped ceiling needs at least 1.60 m of headroom; where the roof slope leaves less, a dormer or raised roof must be added at that spot.

A door under a sloped ceiling whose headroom is under 1.60 m at its wall and within 0.5 m along it must be flagged for a dormer or raised roof; the building stage must not lower the door to the roof line and leave it unusable.

When a bedroom's drawn bed leaves less than the nightstand depth (0.60 m) on one side, the sleeping set is complete with a single nightstand on the free side; do not flag the missing second nightstand as a defect.
A large living room (>= 40 m2) may carry a wardrobe as living_storage; do not flag a wardrobe in a living room of that size as a wrong-type placement.

A wet fixture is typed from the drawn fixture in its own room, not from the size table of a piece in another room; when the plan shows a shower, the wet fixture is a shower even if a size match elsewhere suggests a tub.
An interior bathroom camera must frame the room's full fixture set (WC, basin, storage, bath/shower) from a corner with headroom, never a single fixture in isolation.
A bathroom whose documents draw a tub block (parent-bath set) must be built with a bathtub, not a shower, even when the room is small.
A shoe_cabinet belongs at an entrance hall, not at a top-floor landing; a landing hall takes a console or storage instead.
A balcony/terrace larger than about 12 m2 must be furnished as a seating set (at least two seats plus a table), never a single chair.
A WC flush plate must render as a slim rounded dual-flush plate with a small and a large button, never as a frame holding two flat panes.
An accent wall finish (e.g. vertical slats) is applied to at most one wall of a room, never to all walls of a room or to every room.
An interior camera must frame at least one fixture or piece of value, never a bare wall, corner or switch.
A facade scheme with a stone base and a render body must keep the stone to the base/plinth and apply the render (e.g. white) to the upper walls, never stone from base to eaves.
An interior camera must frame the room's built fixtures; a black/empty view is a camera failure, not a missing room.
A site area drawn in the documents (pool, terrace, parking) must be built with an outline and tracked as a site area, even when its geometry is already present in the model.
The sheets stage must resolve every sheet question before ending; a run that ends 'pending' with open questions has not finished its reading.
A sofa's front is its long side facing the most open room; a front read on its short side (an AI front) is a reading error and must be corrected to the long side.
A drawn piece whose size and wall position match a console table (long, narrow, back on a wall) must be typed console_table, not bench, so its front faces the room and its back rests on the wall.
The big loop must run additional cycles when the first cycle yields no gain, to allow the agent to resolve remaining orientation and placement conflicts.
A sofa drawn with its long side against a wall must have its front facing into the room (away from the wall), not along the long side.
A sofa without a front must have its front set to face the most open floor, towards its partner.
An armchair without a front must have its front set to face away from its wall or towards its partner.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point clear of walls and tall proxies, showing the required elements.
A table_coffee built below the library level must be swapped to a library model that fits the piece's dimensions and room.
A tv_unit built below the library level must be swapped to a library model that fits the piece's dimensions and room.
A tall_cabinet built below the library level must be swapped to a library model that fits the piece's dimensions and room.

When no library model passes the fit rules for a piece, the fitter must not silently keep the parametric mesh as if it were a library pick; it must either relax the height/cap tolerance to accept the nearest library model or flag the piece as unbuildable, never report a library-level build from a parametric fallback.

When a tall piece is placed under a sloped ceiling and its height exceeds the local ceiling clearance, the fitter must either lower the piece to a location with sufficient headroom, swap to a model within the clearance, or flag the placement as infeasible; it must not keep a parametric mesh that violates the ceiling.
A camera of a stair room must be posed from the landing or the hall side so the flight is visible, never from a point inside the stair core.
Views flagged for review are a queue, not a defect; each is resolved by the specific camera or door finding that names it.
Every inside door is built open by default (leaf out of the wall) unless a camera or privacy rule closes it; the build records a leaf state for each door it places.
When a camera looks through an inside door into a room worth showing, the build opens that door (leaf out of the view) and records the state.

A nightstand is placed on the free side of the bed head, not in front of a window; when the bed head is against a window wall the nightstand goes on the opposite side or the window is treated as the head wall.
A toilet is built with its base at floor level (lowest point within -0.005..+0.01 m of the room floor); a model whose base sits above the floor is rejected at fit, not swapped in.
A bathroom washbasin is always built with a mirror above it as part of the vanity set; the bathroom set is incomplete without the mirror.
A tv_unit is placed with its back on a wall; when the only free wall span is blocked by doors or windows, the unit is placed on the next free span or the room is flagged, never left floating.
A coffee table is placed in the seating group with a clear gap to every armchair; when the group is too tight, the armchair is re-posed, not the table pushed into it.
A wardrobe is placed with at least 0.80 m clear in front; when the room cannot give that, the wardrobe is moved to a wall with more clearance or the room is flagged, never left short.
A drawn armchair in a seating group is re-posed (rotated) to face the group and clear its front zone before it is moved; a move beyond the drawn lock is refused, so rotation is the first fix.

findings.message: the judge scores view cam_r_L1_oyun_aktivite_ve_dinlenme_odasi_1 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The render presents a disjointed and poorly styled attic space that fails to meet the project's modern standard. The furniture is a chaotic mix of styles (mid-century, modern, and generic) that do not cohere. The room lacks essential design layers such as a rug, wall art, and proper lighting, leaving the large blue wall and flat ceiling feeling empty and unfinished. The lighting is particularly poor, with a single, weak ceiling fixture creating a flat, uninviting atmosphere compared to the warm, layered lighting in the reference.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_oyun_aktivite_ve_dinlenme_odasi_2 1/5 (a client would not accept it): The render is a failure. It contains a literal 2D image of a table standing on the floor, which is absurd. the judge scores view cam_r_L1_oyun_aktivite_ve_dinlenme_odasi_3 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The room reads as a catalogue of mismatched pieces rather than a designed living space. The dining set (white spindle chair, round pedestal table) and the dark, ornate coffee table with a graffiti-style top clash with the plain grey sofas and the warm, minimal style of the reference. The walls are flat and bare, the floor is a plain plank instead of the herringbone parquet the style calls for, and the curtains are a single flat layer. The result is plain, dated and incoherent.

the judge scores view cam_r_L1_teras_2 2/5 (a client would not accept it): The balcony itself is coherent: the two armchairs (f_L1_108, f_L1_110) and side table (f_L1_109) form a believable, well-scaled seating group, the sliding door (d_L1_003) and window (win_L1_001) read correctly, and the camera (V1) is at a good eye height with the main group in frame. What sinks it is the environment: the view is a flat, empty desert plain with a road and a row of crude, billboard-like 'lollipop' trees, which makes the whole scene look like an unfinished grey-box context rather than a stylish home. The potted plants (f_L1_105/106/107) are also generic and sparse, so the terrace feels plain and cheap for a project that should look designed. The furniture is fine; the world around it is not client-ready.

A stove (hob) that is built into a kitchen counter run is part of that run's model and must not be emitted as a separate scene object; the build stage must suppress a standalone stove object when the stove is a member of a built-in kitchen run, and the conservation check must not flag the run's integrated hob as a missing object.

A kitchen sink that is built into a counter run is part of that run's model and must not be emitted as a separate scene object; the build stage must suppress a standalone sink object when the sink is a member of a built-in kitchen run, and the conservation check must not flag the run's integrated sink as a missing object.

When a drawn piece is a duplicate of a larger drawn piece of the same type (one floor lamp drawn twice, not two), the smaller duplicate is a detail of the larger one and is correctly left out; the reading stage must not flag a same-type duplicate drawn inside its partner as a lost piece.

A stair elevation/section layer (e.g. A-merdiven görünüş) is a drawing of the stair the model already builds; it is not a lost element and must not be reported as unused geometry.

A sanitary-ware layer (e.g. Piu_Vitrifiye) is a drawing of the bathroom fixtures the model already builds; it is not a lost element and must not be reported as unused geometry.

A piece placed by the decor stage must survive the agent stage; if the agent drops it, it must be re-added.

A stove that is a member of a kitchen run (module:kitchen_counter:kitchen_run) must be built as part of that run's model, not as a standalone object; the build stage must emit the run's full model (counter, sink, stove) so every planned member has a scene object.

When two drawn pieces of the same type overlap by more than 30% and one is clearly inside the other, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the same object, not a second piece; the larger is kept and the smaller is dropped as a detail.

When two drawn pieces of the same type overlap by more than 15% and one is clearly inside the other, the smaller is a duplicate drawing of the same object, not a second piece; the larger is kept and the smaller is dropped as a detail.
A small piece drawn 80% or more inside a larger seating piece (armchair, sofa) is its seat cushion or built-in element, not a separate piece; it is dropped as a detail of the larger piece.

A room whose program is a stair core (stair fills the room, no free floor point) is not given an interior camera; it is shown by the adjacent hall's view instead, and the camera stage must skip it rather than report it as a lost view.

A layer whose name is a stair section or elevation view (A-MERDIVEN, A-merdiven görünüş) is a detail view, not plan furniture: the reading classifies it as a detail view and feeds it to the stair reader, and the ledger does not flag it as lost when the stair it documents is built.

A layer whose name is a decorative or sanitary fixture detail view (Deko_Vitrifiye, Piu_Vitrifiye) is a detail view, not plan furniture: the reading classifies it as a detail view and the ledger does not flag it as lost.

rules_proposed.rule: A bath fixture whose height exceeds the sloped-ceiling headroom at its position must not be built as a bathtub; the solver must substitute a shower or a low-profile fixture that fits the available height.

Scene check S1 failures on a level indicate build-stage geometry defects (pieces not resting on the floor, parts detached, or pieces poking through walls); the build stage must be rerun to resolve them.

Scene check S2 failures on a level indicate build-stage geometry defects (pieces not resting on the floor, parts detached, or pieces poking through walls); the build stage must be rerun to resolve them.
A scene check that fails on a level is a build-stage defect: re-run the build stage for that level so the geometry is regenerated and re-checked.

When a seating piece is wedged behind the back of its group and every single rotation is refused (it would face a wall or lose its group), the cause is the room's overall seating layout, not one piece: re-solve the room's AI pieces as a group so the seating cluster is re-placed coherently.

When a TV unit is placed behind the back of a seating piece and rotating it would pull it off its wall (F3) while swapping its model is refused, the cause is the room's seating/TV layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the TV unit lands on a wall facing the sofa.
A piece that crosses a room outline by 0.02 m or less (a few centimetres of its depth) is within tolerance and is not a real finding.

When a coffee table overlaps an armchair and every move of the table is refused (it re-overlaps or hits the max-tries limit), the cause is the seating cluster's spacing: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the table and chairs are placed with clearance.

When a piece's front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door and no single edit can open the path, the cause is the room's circulation layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the walkway is clear.
When a large sofa's front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door, the cause is the room's circulation layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the walkway is clear.

When a seating piece is wedged behind the back of its group and rotating it would face a wall, the cause is the room's overall seating layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the seating cluster is re-placed coherently.

When a TV unit is placed behind the back of a seating piece and rotating it would pull it off its wall while moving it breaks the sofa axis, the cause is the room's seating/TV layout: re-solve the room's AI pieces so the TV unit lands on a wall facing the sofa.
A stove or hob that is part of a kitchen counter run (built into the worktop) is not checked for back-on-wall clearance; the run's own depth against the wall is its position.
A kitchen counter run must leave at least 0.90 m of clear aisle in front of it; if the drawn counter position leaves less, the AI pieces (island, fridge, stools) are re-solved to open the aisle.
A kitchen counter run must leave at least 0.90 m of clear aisle in front of it; if the drawn counter position leaves less, the AI pieces are re-solved to open the aisle.
An armchair in a seating group must face the group's centre (coffee table or sofa); if the drawn position locks it facing away, the AI pieces are re-solved to orient it.
An armchair's front free zone must be clear of other pieces; if the drawn position locks it against a neighbour, the AI pieces are re-solved.
A dining chair needs at least 0.81 m from the table edge to the wall or piece behind it; if the drawn table position leaves less, the AI dining pieces are re-solved.
An armchair in a seating group must face the group's centre; if the drawn position locks it facing away, the AI pieces are re-solved.
An armchair must not stand behind the back of a sofa facing it; it should be on the opposite side of the coffee table or at an angle to the group.
An armchair's front free zone must be clear; if the drawn position locks it against a neighbour, the AI pieces are re-solved.
A double bed needs at least 0.60 m of free aisle on at least one side; if the drawn bed position leaves less, the AI pieces are re-solved to open the aisle.
A wardrobe needs at least 0.80 m of free space in front for the doors to open; if the drawn position leaves less, the AI pieces are re-solved.
A drawn shower with a depth below 0.70 m is a misread; the depth is corrected to the minimum product size (0.70 m) if the room allows.

A bed placed against a wall with a side gap under 0.60 m must be swapped to a narrower model (or the nightstand removed) so the side clearance meets the 0.60 m minimum; a swap to a lower-rated model is refused, so pick the narrowest model in the project's style chain.

A wardrobe whose front clearance is under 0.80 m and whose drawn wall span is blocked by doors/windows must be slid along its wall (or to the nearest free span) so the door opens; if no span within 1.2 m of the drawn place is free, the room layout must be re-solved rather than forcing the piece off its wall.
A bed with a side gap under 0.60 m that cannot be fixed by moving (headboard must stay on the wall) must be swapped to a narrower model in the project's style chain.
A wardrobe with under 0.80 m front clearance that cannot be slid along its wall (no free span) must be moved to the nearest free place in the room so the door opens.
A piece blocking the free zone in front of a sofa must be moved (or removed) so the sofa's front use zone is clear; the blocking piece, not the sofa, is the cause.
A coffee table not in front of the sofa must be moved to the sofa's front use zone (0.40-0.60 m from the seat front), aligned with the sofa's long side.
An armchair more than 2.50 m from the coffee table or more than 30° off its axis must be moved into the seating group (within 2.50 m, within 30° of the table axis).
An armchair standing behind the back of its group's anchor must be rotated to face the group (the anchor's front), not the anchor's back.

A drawn coffee table that is not in front of the sofa and cannot be moved more than 0.3 m (drawn lock) must have the sofa moved to the table, or the table re-anchored, so the table sits in the sofa's front zone.
A flat 2D image of furniture standing on the floor is a rendering error, not a real piece; it must be removed (or replaced by a real 3D model of the same type).
An armchair standing behind the back of its group's anchor must be rotated to face the group.
A dining chair with under 0.81 m behind it (to the wall or a piece) must be moved so the pull-out clearance meets 0.81 m.
A tv_unit whose back is not on a wall (more than 0.05 m off) must be moved to a wall so its back rests on it.
Armchairs facing the back of a tv_unit that is off the wall are a symptom of the tv_unit's position; move the tv_unit to the wall so the armchairs face its front.

When multiple pieces in a room face each other's backs (a seating group with reversed orientations), the room's AI pieces must be re-laid out as a group so the seating faces the tv_unit/anchor, not each other's backs.
A built piece must not cross its room outline; when the assigned model is too deep for the wall bay, swap to a model whose depth fits the bay.
A drawn sofa footprint whose width exceeds its depth (an L or corner shape) must be typed as sofa_corner, not sofa, so the built model matches the drawn shape.
A seating group's front use zone must be kept clear; when a piece blocks the sofa's front, the room is re-laid out so the group faces open floor.
A seating group's front use zone must be kept clear; when a piece blocks an armchair's front, the room is re-laid out so the group faces open floor.
A kitchen run must leave at least 0.90 m of aisle in front of the counter; when the room is too narrow for the drawn run plus aisle, the run is re-solved on the longest free wall span.
A seating group's members must face the group; when an armchair does not face its group, the room is re-laid out so the group is coherent.
A double bed must have at least 0.60 m of free walkway on each side; when the room is too narrow for the bed plus two 0.60 m aisles, the bed is placed against a wall with one side open.
A decor item that cannot rest on its host within tolerance is correctly dropped; the host's top surface must be flat and clear.
A fixture under a sloped ceiling is capped at the slope height at its footprint; the cap is independent of the drawn size check, so a size refusal must not block the height fix.
Scene geometry checks (S1) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S2) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S4) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S6) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
A scene check that fails on a level must be re-run after the level's pieces are corrected; the build stage owns the scene assembly.
When an armchair's orientation is refused because rotating it breaks its group facing, the whole seating group must be re-solved so the armchair faces the group and the coffee table.
A tv_unit that stands behind the back of a seat and cannot be rotated without leaving the room outline must be re-placed by the room solver so its back is on a wall and it faces the seating.
A wardrobe that pokes through the room outline by a few centimetres should be swapped for a model whose depth fits the wall bay.
